idiom_name: public template method + private/protected `*_impl` hook (Module#prepend for wrapping)
implementation_notes: Ruby's visibility is enforced by the call-site receiver rule: a private method may only be called without an explicit receiver (or with literal self), which is exactly what lets the base class call read_impl on itself while clients cannot. Declare the entry point public, keep the hooks private (protected where sibling instances must call them), and remember that private does not mean non-overridable - a subclass can still redefine the public method, so this is visibility plus convention, not a guarantee. Module#prepend with super is the Ruby-idiomatic way to add behaviour around an existing method without touching the hierarchy.
code_sketch:
class Reader
  def read(stream)                 # public, stable entry point
    raise ArgumentError, 'stream required' unless stream
    read_impl(stream)              # implicit receiver: private hook is callable
  end

  private

  def read_impl(stream)
    raise NotImplementedError
  end
end
pitfalls: private is a call-site rule, not an encapsulation boundary: send, public_send or instance_eval reach the hook from outside.
A subclass may widen a hook's visibility back to public, re-exposing the extension point to clients.
method_missing / respond_to_missing? overrides can make the entry point appear to exist while hook lookup changes silently - keep metaprogramming away from the wrapper.
